tek_cumle: To understand a film is to see what its elements do within the whole, how they repeat, and how they return transformed; every concept you learned this week serves this single skill.

bolumler.html:
We are wrapping up Week 1. First, take the 10-question multiple-choice test on the week’s concepts without looking at the book; then write answers to the syllabus’s three short-answer questions and complete the analysis task. The point is not to earn a grade but to see which concepts haven’t settled in yet.

  • Several options may look “partly right”; choose the one that expresses the concept most completely.
  • Bordwell and Thompson’s concepts are descriptive; be suspicious of options that contain value judgments.
  • Some questions are asked through Citizen Kane: knowing the name of a principle isn’t enough — you need to be able to see it in a scene.

Phase note: Phase I (Foundations, Weeks 1–5) has begun; the phase exam comes at the end of Week 5. In Week 2 we move on to narrative.

quiz.soru: According to Bordwell and Thompson, which three dimensions must be considered together to understand cinema?
secenekler: Screenplay, acting and music
Creativity (art), technology and industry
Director, producer and audience
Image, sound and editing
quiz.aciklama: Creative decisions are made within technological possibilities and an industrial order; the other options are components of a film.

quiz.soru: What is the most accurate explanation of the movement we see on the screen?
secenekler: The film strip contains a single, continuously moving image
Our visual system perceives still frames shown in rapid succession as movement
The flicker of the projector tires the eye and creates a sense of movement
We see movement on screen because the camera moves constantly during shooting
quiz.aciklama: Apparent motion: it arises from our motion perception fusing still frames; we see movement even when the camera is stationary.

quiz.soru: Which is the correct order of the stages of production?
secenekler: Shooting → screenplay and financing → preparation → editing
Preparation → screenplay and financing → editing → shooting
Screenplay and financing → preproduction → production → editing and assembly (postproduction)
Screenplay → editing → preparation → shooting
quiz.aciklama: Script and money → preparation → shooting → editing and sound; then distribution and exhibition.

quiz.soru: Why do Bordwell and Thompson find the form/content distinction misleading?
secenekler: Content is unimportant; only form matters
Form is merely visual style and has nothing to do with content
What we think of as content (subject, theme, character) gains meaning and effect only within form, through the relationships among elements
Every film’s content is actually the same
quiz.aciklama: Form is not a container for content; the same story told in a different order or from a different point of view is a different experience. Option A simply reverses the distinction and still splits the film in two.

quiz.soru: Which of the following is NOT one of the five principles of a formal system?
secenekler: Function
Similarity and repetition
Realism
Development
quiz.aciklama: The five principles are: function; similarity and repetition; difference and variation; development; unity/disunity. Realism belongs to debates about style and theory (Weeks 10–12).

quiz.soru: What does it mean to look at the newsreel section of Citizen Kane through the principle of “function”?
secenekler: Assessing whether it is technically well shot
Asking what job it does within the whole: e.g., giving the viewer the outline of a life while leaving the central question open
Researching whether it was taken from a real newsreel
Deciding whether it is our favorite part of the film
quiz.aciklama: The newsreel gives the outer contours of the life but doesn’t explain what the last word means; it sets the investigation in motion. A and D are value judgments; C is a question of production history.

quiz.soru: What is the effect called when a film deliberately frustrates an expectation it has built?
secenekler: Surprise
Suspense
Curiosity
Motif
quiz.aciklama: When an expectation is overturned, we get surprise; when it is delayed, suspense; a question about past events we haven’t been shown produces curiosity.

quiz.soru: In formal analysis, what is a “motif”?
secenekler: The film’s main theme
The director’s reason for making the film
An element (image, object, line of dialogue, sound, color, etc.) that recurs meaningfully throughout the film
A striking object that appears only once in a scene
quiz.aciklama: The motif is the most concrete form of the principle of repetition; don’t confuse it with “motivation.”

quiz.soru: What is the most practical way to examine the pattern of development?
secenekler: Measuring the film’s running time
Comparing the beginning with the end and tracing the path between them (a journey, an investigation, a timeline)
Examining only the most exciting scene
Looking at box-office returns
quiz.aciklama: Comparing beginning and end makes the path the film follows visible; this is exactly what the analysis task asks for.

quiz.soru: From a formal point of view, how should we assess some questions being left unanswered?
secenekler: It is always a flaw
It has nothing to do with form; it is a problem with the screenplay
Unity is never total; some loose ends can work as deliberate disunity
It shows that the viewer misunderstood the film
quiz.aciklama: Unity is a matter of degree; disunity is not in itself a defect.

sorular: Why is the form/content distinction misleading? Explain in your own words, with an example from a film (4–6 sentences).
List the five principles of a formal system and define each in a single sentence.
How do expectation and surprise work in form? Show the difference between suspense, surprise and curiosity with one example of each.
analiz:
Task: Compare the opening and the ending of Citizen Kane through the principles of repetition and variation. 600–900 words.

Preparation: Rewatch the first and last five minutes or so back to back. For each, make a list: places, objects, written words, sounds; where the camera starts and where it goes; lighting and music.

  1. Repetition: At least three concrete elements from the opening that return in the ending.
  2. Variation: How do these elements change when they return? Look at the direction of the camera’s movement, the order of the elements, and what the viewer now knows.
  3. Expectation: What question does the opening set up? Does the ending give the same answer to the viewer and to the characters? What does that difference mean?
  4. Development and unity: What shape does the echo between opening and ending give the film? Does the film close, or does it leave a deliberate loose end?
  5. Form and meaning: How does this pattern relate to what the film says about knowing another person? Discuss it without separating “content” from “form.”

Criteria: concrete observation; correct use of concepts; explaining what the differences accomplish; a persuasive link between form and meaning. Write your own analysis before reading any commentary.
gozlem: Compare the first and last 30 seconds of an episode of a series or a short video you watched this week: does an element seen at the start (a place, a piece of music, a line of dialogue) return at the end? How has it changed? Note it down in two sentences.

terimler.tanim: The reappearance of an element across a film, building a pattern.
The return of a recurring element in altered form; meaning often arises from this difference.
An image, object, sound or line of dialogue that recurs meaningfully throughout a film.
The pattern that elements follow from beginning to end; it becomes visible when the beginning is compared with the end.
Effects created when an expectation is overturned, delayed, or left open with respect to past events.
How tightly a film’s elements are bound together; loose ends can be a deliberate choice.

yarin: Week 2 begins: Narrative. We start with the difference between story (fabula) and plot (syuzhet); the film of the week is Rashomon (Kurosawa, 1950).
